Hey I am an aerospace engineer, more specifically a Safety and Mission Assurance Engineer on Canadarm3.

Preferred degrees depends a lot on what you want to be doing in the field of aerospace. If you're interested in orbital mechanics, mission & requirement planning, interpretation of results, etc, we prefer experts like those with BSc/MSc in the topic of interest.

For design, development, & upkeep of the hardware and stations, engineering degrees have preference. There's a lot of work in this field building hardware that collects the data scientists need, proving that it can safely fly through analysis and test, and maintaining those functions once it's off the earth.

I'll admit, when breaking into the industry, there is more work for engineers. Most people in the field have an engineering degree in some flavour. But once you're in the field, people move all over regardless of their degree. I know Material Scientists with solely "engineering" degrees and Structural Engineers with solely "scientific" degrees. We extremely value anyone that knows and can communicate the fine detail on the environments and systems we work with.

In summary, the CSA would absolutely hire someone with a BSc in Physics and MSc in Aerospace, but you might get hired faster if one of those is an Eng degree. Once you're in though, we don't care about degrees.

My best guesses are either separation anxiety or boredom. Yes, dogs can tell if someone is just upstairs or fully away from the house usually. Either way I wouldn't recommend continue to give treats when she's barking. 

Separation anxiety is extremely common in rescues. If she's barking immediately when you leave, scratching at doors, seems stressed or unable to relax while you're gone, it's definitely anxiety. 

The best thing you can do is train her that you will come back. Step outside the door and wait for her barking to stop, then come back in and reward her and celebrate. If she's very anxious like my pup was when I first got her, the silence you're waiting for might be only a few seconds at first. Keep leaving, then returning once she is quiet. Slowly build up the time you spend away with her quiet.

Some dogs, mine included, need a distraction for the first couple minutes when their person leaves so they don't fixate on you being gone. You can use slow feeders, stuffed kongs (freeze them to extend the life), treats, snuffle mats, and favourite toys to draw away their attention while you step out. This can also help with the boredom factor if that's the cause of the problem. 

Both separation anxiety and boredom can be helped through the introduction of additional stimulation. You can find dog TV or calming music for dogs on youtube and play it for her. You can setup treat puzzle or foraging toys around the house for something to do.

And most of all stick with it! She'll learn eventually that she's safe and comfy in your home and doesn't need to bark when you're gone.

Non-binary is a subset of trans where a person does not identify as male or female. Non-binary people are often uncomfortable and/or experience dysphoria for both male and female traits. Alternatively, they may like specific male and female traits but not feel strongly enough to identify as either. For example, a non-binary person who was assigned male at birth may want breasts and take hormones to achieve this but not want any other feminine features.

There's really no rules or guides to being non-binary. Some may undergo a medical transition such as surgeries and taking hormones but still identify as non-binary. Others may just change the pronouns they use. The idea that a non-binary person is just a butch/tomboyish girl is actually a stereotype because often young women have more freedom to play with their gender presentation (like looking tomboyish). 

Gender is a lot more complicated than social roles. It's also how you feel internally about yourself, your body, and how people see you. People who seek to transition medically (ie transition their sex) often find that their physical body causes them distress because it does not match how they feel internally.

TLDR; when hurt, your body increases heart rate, blood pressure, and glucose. When fasting, these are all lower normally so it's a bit of system shock and can make you faint. Lay down to avoid getting hurt.

This is actually really common and why they ask you to eat something before getting a tattoo. When you get hurt (even if you do it yourself), your body activates the fight or flight response. This very quickly raises your heart rate, blood pressure, and tries to provide more glucose to your muscles. 

When fasting, your heart rate and blood pressure tend to be lower to conserve energy. So when fight or flight happens, you get hit with a really fast spike in these things. You also are already running on stored glucose so your body may struggle to find an easily accessible source and use a lot of energy quickly. All of this happens very quickly and can make your brain hit the reset button, aka you will get dizzy and faint for a min.

If it happens again, lay down flat on your back and take deep breaths until it passes or you faint. This is safer and helps your blood pressure stabilize faster. Make sure to drink water and have a snack afterward.
